questions.q: What is "data leakage" in a machine learning pipeline?
options: When a dataset file is accidentally shared publicly
When information that wouldn't legitimately be available at real prediction time improperly influences training or evaluation, inflating performance
When a model trains too slowly
When a column is renamed incorrectly
questions.explain: Data leakage is specifically about information leaking into the training or evaluation process that wouldn't genuinely be available at the moment a real prediction needs to be made.

questions.q: Why is data leakage considered uniquely dangerous compared to most other ML mistakes?
options: It always crashes the training process immediately, so it's easy to catch
It makes a model look better than it actually is during development, only to fail once the leaked information isn't available in production
It only affects regression models, never classification
It is impossible to detect under any circumstances
questions.explain: Unlike most mistakes, which visibly hurt performance, leakage makes results look artificially strong during development — the danger shows up later, when the model fails in the real world without the leaked information.

questions.q: In the lesson's loan default example, why is a feature like "days_to_payoff" a case of target leakage?
options: Because it's a categorical feature
Because it only gets set after a default has already happened, effectively encoding the outcome itself
Because it has too many missing values
Because it's measured in days instead of months
questions.explain: A feature that's only populated after the outcome occurs is really a disguised version of the label — of course it predicts default well, since it's generated by the default happening in the first place.

questions.q: What kind of leakage does using next month's usage data to predict this month's churn represent?
options: Group leakage
Temporal leakage — using information from the future relative to the actual prediction point
Train/test contamination
This is not an example of leakage
questions.explain: At the real moment you'd need to predict this month's churn, next month hasn't happened yet — using it anyway is temporal leakage, common in time-series and forecasting problems.

questions.q: What single question does the lesson offer as a way to catch nearly every form of leakage?
options: Is the dataset large enough?
For this feature, would you genuinely have this information at the moment you'd actually need to make the prediction in the real world?
Did the model take longer than an hour to train?
Is the feature numeric or categorical?
questions.explain: Checking whether a feature would genuinely be available at real prediction time catches target leakage, temporal leakage, and most other disguised forms, regardless of how clean the surrounding code looks.
